1→# Dispute Resolution Policy — Ryde (Singapore)
   2→
   3→**Version 1.0 · effective 2026-09-21 · applies to on-demand trips in Singapore**
   4→
   5→This document is the rule set the Judge agent applies. It is **data, not code**: the pipeline
   6→reads it at a known path, agents cite rules by ID, and a different policy document drops in
   7→with no code change.
   8→
   9→---
  10→
  11→## PROVENANCE — read this before citing anything here
  12→
  13→**This document was synthesised by the project team. It is NOT an official Ryde document and
  14→was not supplied by the organisers.** It is built in three layers, and every rule below is
  15→tagged with which layer it comes from:
  16→
  17→| Tag | Meaning |
  18→|---|---|
  19→| **[RYDE-ACTUAL]** | Taken from Ryde's own published policy pages or Terms of Use. The rule states what Ryde actually publishes, with the source URL. |
  20→| **[PEER-DERIVED]** | Ryde publishes no rule here. The rule is modelled on a comparable Singapore operator's published policy (Grab or TADA), cited, and adapted. |
  21→| **[SYNTHESISED]** | Neither Ryde nor its peers publish a usable rule. The team authored it. These are the rules a real Ryde policy would most likely word differently. |
  22→
  23→**Why a synthesised policy exists at all.** The challenge statement requires the Judge to apply
  24→"company policy", and no policy document was supplied. Rather than invent one from nothing, the
  25→team researched Ryde's actual published policies first (help centre, Terms of Use, press
  26→statements), used Grab and TADA as peer references for the gaps, and authored only what neither
  27→publishes. The three-layer tagging exists so a reader can always tell which is which.
  28→
  29→**The honest limitation.** Ryde's public material covers cancellation and waiting fees in
  30→detail, and covers route deviation and driver no-show barely at all. Section 3 (route deviation)
  31→is therefore mostly **[SYNTHESISED]**, and that is the section carrying the most invention. Ryde's
  32→Terms of Use additionally **disclaim** an adjudication role (Section A Clause 10: "Any complaints
  33→between Partners and Users must be taken up with each other directly"), so an automated Judge is
  34→a design this project proposes, not a process Ryde publishes.
  35→
  36→**Fee figures drift.** Ryde's rider-side and driver-side pages currently disagree ($6.61/$5.00
  37→versus $4.50/$4.50) and the cancellation fee has moved $4.30 → $5.30 → $6.50 → $6.61 since 2017.
  38→This document uses the **rider-side current figures**, corroborated by the waiver voucher amount,
  39→retrieved 2026-09-21. Treat every amount in the parameters table as swappable.
  40→
  41→**Sources.** Ryde: `help.rydesharing.com` cancellation and waiting fee policy, waiver request
  42→pages, Driver Performance and Community Standards, `rydesharing.com/terms-of-use/`. Peers:
  43→`grab.com/sg/cancellationpolicy/`, Grab Transport Terms of Service, TADA Singapore rider FAQ and
  44→T&C. Regulatory: LTA/PTC joint statement on fare accuracy, CaseTrust-LTA accreditation standards.
  45→Full citations with retrieval dates are in the research reports the team holds.
  46→
  47→---
  48→
  49→## Parameters
  50→
  51→Amounts and thresholds are collected here so they can be changed in one place. Rules reference
  52→them by name.
  53→
  54→| Parameter | Value | Layer | Note |
  55→|---|---|---|---|
  56→| Cancellation fee | SGD 6.61 | [RYDE-ACTUAL] | Rider-side published figure |
  57→| Waiting time fee | SGD 5.00 | [RYDE-ACTUAL] | Charged at trip end |
  58→| Free cancellation window | 3 minutes after matching | [RYDE-ACTUAL] | On-demand trips |
  59→| Minimum driver wait before no-show | 3 minutes after "I'm Here" | [RYDE-ACTUAL] | |
  60→| Driver proximity limit at pickup | 500 metres | [PEER-DERIVED] | TADA's published figure |
  61→| Material route deviation | 20% and 1.0 km | [SYNTHESISED] | Both must be met |
  62→| Gross route deviation | 5.0 km | [SYNTHESISED] | Material regardless of percentage |
  63→| De minimis adjustment | SGD 1.00 | [SYNTHESISED] | Below this, no monetary remedy |
  64→| Autonomous decision cap | SGD 50.00 | [SYNTHESISED] | Above this, human review |
  65→| Filing window | 30 days from the trip | [RYDE-ACTUAL] | Waiver request pages |
  66→
  67→---
  68→
  69→## 1. Scope and general rules
  70→
  71→### GEN-1 — What this policy covers [SYNTHESISED]
  72→
  73→This policy governs two dispute categories on Singapore on-demand trips: **route deviation /
  74→overcharged fare** (Section 3) and **no-show charge / cancellation fee** (Section 4). Any other
  75→dispute — property damage, cleaning, safety incidents, lost items, promotions, or anything the
  76→filing party selects as "other" — is outside this policy and goes to human review under ESC-1.
  77→
  78→RydeTAXI trips are excluded from Section 4 entirely: metered taxi services do not carry Ryde's
  79→cancellation and waiting fee policy ("Cancellation Policy applies to all Service Types in the
  80→Ryde app... All services except RydeTAXI", Ryde help centre) [RYDE-ACTUAL]. Cite `service_type`.
  81→Where `service_type` is absent from the pack's citable refs, the record did not state which
  82→service was booked: the exclusion cannot be applied and the dispute proceeds on the merits. Do not
  83→cite a field that is not in the citable list — an unresolvable citation is recorded as ungrounded.
  84→
  85→### GEN-2 — Every finding must rest on the Evidence Pack [SYNTHESISED]
  86→
  87→Quantitative facts come only from the deterministic Evidence Pack, cited by field reference. A
  88→party's assertion is not a fact: it is a claim to be tested against the pack. Where a pack field
  89→needed to decide a rule is `null`, the rule is **not satisfied and not refuted** — it is
  90→undetermined, and ESC-2 applies.
  91→
  92→No agent computes its own numbers. A ruling that relies on arithmetic not present in the pack is
  93→invalid regardless of whether the arithmetic is correct.
  94→
  95→### GEN-3 — Burden of proof sits with the charge, not the rider [PEER-DERIVED]
  96→
  97→Where a fee has been charged to a party, the **records must positively support the charge**. If
  98→the preconditions for the fee cannot be shown from the Evidence Pack, the fee is not valid and is
  99→refunded. Grab states this directly for cancellation fees: "You will not be charged the $4
 100→cancellation fee if any of the above are not fulfilled"
 101→(`grab.com/sg/cancellationpolicy/`). The same principle is applied here to Ryde's fees.
 102→
 103→This rule does **not** mean the rider always wins. It means the platform's own logs must show the
 104→fee was earned. Where they do, the fee stands and the claim fails.
 105→
 106→### GEN-4 — De minimis [SYNTHESISED]
 107→
 108→Where the computed monetary remedy is below the de minimis amount (SGD 1.00), no monetary
 109→adjustment is made. The finding is still recorded and explained to both parties, and the
 110→behavioural consequences in GEN-7 still apply. A fifty-cent refund costs more to administer than
 111→it returns.
 112→
 113→### GEN-5 — Form of remedy [SYNTHESISED, grounded in observed practice]
 114→
 115→Refunds of **fees** (cancellation, waiting, no-show) are issued as **Ryde wallet credit**. This
 116→follows Ryde's published waiver practice: an eligible waiver request produces "a voucher with a
 117→unique code worth $6.61 as a refund for the incurred Cancellation Charges" (Ryde help centre).
 118→
 119→Refunds of **fare overcharges** are issued to the **original payment method** where the trip was
 120→paid by card, and as wallet credit where it was paid by cash or wallet. Ryde's Terms of Use
 121→reserve "absolute discretion to any refunds" and allow either route (Section A Clause 7.2); the
 122→split above is the team's rule, not Ryde's, and is chosen so an overcharge is made whole in the
 123→currency it was taken in.
 124→
 125→### GEN-6 — Filing window [RYDE-ACTUAL]
 126→
 127→A dispute must be filed within **30 days of the trip**. Ryde's waiver pages are explicit:
 128→"Requests submitted after 30 days of the trip will not be considered for waivers." A dispute
 129→filed outside the window is declined on that ground alone, without reaching the merits.
 130→
 131→Cite `filing.days_since_trip`. Where `filing.window_established` is false the pack could not
 132→measure the interval: do not decline on this ground — decide the merits instead. Declining a valid
 133→claim on an unverified technicality is the worse error.
 134→
 135→### GEN-7 — Findings against a party are recorded, not punished here [RYDE-ACTUAL]
 136→
 137→This policy decides money. It does not suspend accounts. Where a ruling finds conduct that Ryde's
 138→Driver Performance and Community Standards treat as a violation — "Remaining stationary and
 139→uncontactable after accepting a ride to trigger cancellation or waiting fees", "Abuse of
 140→Cancellation and Waiting Fee Policy", or overcharging riders — the ruling records the finding and
 141→flags it for the platform's own enforcement process. Suspension thresholds (driver rating below
 142→4.80, cancellation rate above 17.5%) are the platform's to apply, not this policy's.
 143→
 144→### GEN-8 — Behavioural history is context, never the deciding factor [SYNTHESISED]
 145→
 146→Party profiles (dispute rate, upheld rate, rating, tenure) may be cited as context and may inform
 147→confidence. They must **never** be the reason a claim succeeds or fails. A rider with a high
 148→dispute rate can still be overcharged; a driver with a perfect record can still take a detour. Use
 149→history only to break a tie the evidence leaves genuinely even, and say so explicitly when you do.
 150→
 151→### GEN-9 — Chat signals are weak evidence [SYNTHESISED]
 152→
 153→The chat lexicon counts in the Evidence Pack are a deterministic keyword heuristic, not a trained
 154→model, and the pack labels them as such. They may corroborate a finding — for example, a rider
 155→questioning the route while it was happening supports that the deviation was unannounced — but a
 156→keyword count alone never establishes a fact and never carries a ruling on its own.
 157→
 158→---
 159→
 160→## 2. Evidence standards
 161→
 162→### EV-1 — What the records must show for a fare finding [SYNTHESISED]
 163→
 164→A route-deviation or overcharge finding requires, at minimum: the trip's GPS trace or a recorded
 165→actual distance (`route.actual_distance_km`), the quoted or estimated distance
 166→(`route.estimated_distance_km`), and the fare charged (`fare.charged_sgd`). Without all three,
 167→the deviation cannot be measured and ESC-2 applies.
 168→
 169→Where GPS points are present, the actual distance is the haversine sum over consecutive points and
 170→is preferred over any distance asserted in the record. A trace containing an unusable point — not an
 171→object, or coordinates missing, non-numeric, non-finite, or out of range — has an **unknown** length,
 172→not a shorter one: the distance fields are null with a note naming the point, no distance is
 173→substituted from elsewhere in the record, and ESC-2 applies.
 174→
 175→### EV-2 — What the records must show for a no-show finding [RYDE-ACTUAL + PEER-DERIVED]
 176→
 177→A no-show charge requires the platform's own timestamps: when the driver marked arrival
 178→(`cancellation.driver_arrived_at`), when the trip was cancelled (`cancellation.cancelled_at`),
 179→and the resulting wait (`cancellation.driver_wait_minutes`). Where the driver's position at
 180→arrival and the booked pickup point are both recorded, the distance between them
 181→(`cancellation.driver_distance_from_pickup_m`) is decisive under NS-3.
 182→
 183→Ryde requires the driver to press "I'm Here" and wait more than 3 minutes before a no-show
 184→cancellation is chargeable [RYDE-ACTUAL]. The GPS proximity requirement is peer-derived: Grab
 185→requires the driver to be "at the pick-up location according to GPS data", and TADA uses a 500
 186→metre radius.
 187→
 188→### EV-3 — Fare arithmetic must reconcile [SYNTHESISED]
 189→
 190→Where the fare breakdown is present, its components must sum to the amount charged
 191→(`fare.breakdown_consistent`). An inconsistent breakdown is itself evidence of an incorrect
 192→charge and is grounds for a finding under RD-5, independent of any route question.
 193→
 194→Tolls, ERP charges and entry fees are legitimately **excluded from the quoted fare and added on
 195→top** ("Surcharges such as toll charges, overtime fees and valet parking fees are excluded from
 196→the base fare", Ryde help centre) [RYDE-ACTUAL]. Their presence in a breakdown is not by itself an
 197→overcharge. Their presence where no such charge could have been incurred is.
 198→
 199→---
 200→
 201→## 3. Route deviation and overcharged fare
 202→
 203→Ryde publishes no route-deviation policy. What it does publish is the fixed-fare principle —
 204→"Fares quoted for our services are generally fixed, except for RydeTAXI" [RYDE-ACTUAL] — and a
 205→fraud rule treating "overcharging riders or manipulating fares" as grounds for suspension
 206→[RYDE-ACTUAL]. Grab's position, the closest peer statement, is that "drivers have the right to
 207→take the fastest or shortest route available as recommended by the GPS for fixed-fare rides"
 208→[PEER-DERIVED]. Everything below builds the actual test from those three anchors.
 209→
 210→### RD-1 — When a deviation is material [SYNTHESISED]
 211→
 212→A route deviation is **material** when either:
 213→
 214→- `route.deviation_pct` is at least 20% **and** `route.deviation_km` is at least 1.0 km; or
 215→- `route.deviation_km` is at least 5.0 km, whatever the percentage.
 216→
 217→Both limbs exist because neither works alone. A percentage alone fires on a 2 km trip that went
 218→400 metres wide, which is noise. A distance alone never fires on a short trip, where a 1.5 km
 219→detour is the whole journey again.
 220→
 221→A deviation below both limbs is **immaterial**: drivers exercise routing judgement, and a policy
 222→that treats every variance as a breach would make normal driving a violation.
 223→
 224→### RD-2 — A material deviation is not automatically a breach [PEER-DERIVED]
 225→
 226→A material deviation is justified, and no remedy is due, where any of the following is shown:
 227→
 228→- The rider requested or agreed to the route or a change of destination. The intake form answer
 229→  on route agreement and the chat log's agreement markers are the evidence.
 230→- The rider added a stop or changed the drop-off point during the trip. Ryde has adjusted fares on
 231→  exactly this basis: "the drop-off location was changed from the initially booked
 232→  [destination]... the trip fare has been adjusted accordingly" [RYDE-ACTUAL, press statement].
 233→- A road closure, diversion or comparable condition made the expected route unavailable, and the
 234→  driver stated it at the time rather than afterwards.
 235→
 236→Congestion alone does **not** justify a material deviation in distance. Traffic is a reason a
 237→route takes longer, not a reason it becomes physically longer. A driver who reroutes around
 238→congestion and thereby drives materially further has made a routing choice the rider did not buy.
 239→
 240→### RD-3 — Unjustified material deviation: remedy [SYNTHESISED]
 241→
 242→Where a deviation is material under RD-1 and unjustified under RD-2, the rider is refunded the
 243→**fare consequence of the deviation**: `fare.deviation_fare_delta_sgd`, being what the trip as
 244→driven cost minus what the expected route would have cost.
 245→
 246→The remedy is the delta, not the whole fare. The rider received the journey and owes its proper
 247→price; what they do not owe is the cost of distance they did not ask for. Where the delta is below
 248→the de minimis amount, GEN-4 applies and no money moves.
 249→
 250→Where the delta cannot be computed but an overcharge is otherwise established, the remedy is
 251→`fare.difference_sgd` if positive, and otherwise the dispute escalates under ESC-2 rather than
 252→resolving on a guessed figure.
 253→
 254→### RD-4 — Deviation with no fare consequence [SYNTHESISED]
 255→
 256→A trip may deviate materially and cost the rider nothing extra, because the fare was genuinely
 257→fixed at booking. Where `fare.deviation_fare_delta_sgd` is zero or negative, or the charged amount
 258→matches the quoted fare, the correct outcome is **no action on the money**, with an explanation
 259→that the fixed fare protected the rider and the routing is recorded under GEN-7.
 260→
 261→Do not manufacture a refund to satisfy a complaint. A rider who was not charged more was not
 262→overcharged, and saying so plainly is a better answer than a goodwill payment that implies a
 263→wrong.
 264→
 265→### RD-5 — Overcharge independent of routing [RYDE-ACTUAL + SYNTHESISED]
 266→
 267→A fare may be wrong without any deviation. Where `fare.breakdown_consistent` is false, or
 268→`fare.difference_sgd` is materially positive against the recomputed fare at the recorded tariff
 269→rates, the rider is refunded the difference regardless of the route taken.
 270→
 271→Singapore's regulator has put fare accuracy squarely on the operator: in the 2024 ERP
 272→mis-rating case the LTA and PTC stated that "operators of ride-hail services are responsible for
 273→ensuring that accurate fares are charged to passengers", and directed a full audit and
 274→reimbursement [PEER-DERIVED, regulatory]. A pricing error is the platform's to fix, not the
 275→rider's to absorb and not the driver's to pay for.
 276→
 277→### RD-6 — Duration overrun is not, by itself, a fare dispute [SYNTHESISED]
 278→
 279→A trip that took longer than estimated without travelling materially further
 280→(`duration.delta_pct` high, `route.deviation_pct` low) is a traffic outcome, not a deviation.
 281→Where the fare includes a time component and the delay was not the driver's doing, the time charge
 282→stands.
 283→
 284→The exception is a delay the driver caused — an unnecessary stop, or a detour that also cost time.
 285→There, the time component of the deviation is already inside
 286→`fare.deviation_fare_delta_sgd` and is remedied by RD-3 rather than separately.
 287→
 288→---
 289→
 290→## 4. No-show charge and cancellation fee
 291→
 292→This is the section where Ryde's own published policy is strongest, and most of what follows is
 293→[RYDE-ACTUAL]. The gap Ryde leaves — what a rider is owed when the **driver** fails to appear —
 294→is filled from Grab and TADA.
 295→
 296→### NS-1 — When a cancellation fee is chargeable to the rider [RYDE-ACTUAL]
 297→
 298→Ryde's published rule, verbatim: "All cancellations made within 3 minutes of matching are not
 299→chargeable. Rider will be charged a Cancellation Fee of $6.61 if: Rider cancels after 3 minutes of
 300→matching OR the driver presses 'I'm Here', waits for > 3 minutes for the rider to arrive at the
 301→pick-up point and cancels the trip (Rider NO SHOW and no trip completion)."
 302→
 303→Two distinct routes to the same fee, and they are tested differently. A rider-initiated
 304→cancellation turns on elapsed time from matching: cite `cancellation.matching_to_cancel_minutes`,
 305→and where it is at or below **3 minutes** the fee is not chargeable regardless of anything else.
 306→Check `cancellation.matching_anchor_source` before relying on a borderline figure: where it reads
 307→`trip.requested_at` the interval was measured from booking rather than matching, so the true
 308→interval is shorter than shown and a figure just above 3 minutes does not establish a chargeable
 309→cancellation. A driver-initiated no-show cancellation turns on the driver having actually arrived
 310→and actually waited, which NS-2 and NS-3 test.
 311→
 312→### NS-2 — The wait must be real [RYDE-ACTUAL]
 313→
 314→For a driver-initiated no-show charge, `cancellation.driver_wait_minutes` must exceed **3
 315→minutes**, measured from the driver marking arrival. A cancellation inside 3 minutes of arrival
 316→does not earn the fee, and the fee is refunded in full.
 317→
 318→Where the wait cannot be established from the timestamps, the fee is not supported and GEN-3
 319→applies: the charge fails for want of proof rather than succeeding by default.
 320→
 321→### NS-3 — The driver must have been at the pickup point [PEER-DERIVED]
 322→
 323→Where the records show the driver's position at the moment of arrival, that position must be
 324→within **500 metres** of the booked pickup point
 325→(`cancellation.driver_distance_from_pickup_m`). Beyond that, the driver was not at the pickup
 326→point, the "I'm Here" mark does not reflect arrival, and **the no-show fee is invalid and refunded
 327→in full** — regardless of how long the subsequent "wait" ran.
 328→
 329→This is the rule that catches the failure mode both Ryde and its peers acknowledge: a driver who
 330→marks arrival from elsewhere and lets the clock run. Ryde's own standards prohibit "Remaining
 331→stationary and uncontactable after accepting a ride to trigger cancellation or waiting fees"
 332→[RYDE-ACTUAL]. Grab requires the driver to be "at the pick-up location according to GPS data" and
 333→TADA uses a 500 metre radius; the figure here is TADA's [PEER-DERIVED].
 334→
 335→A driver marking arrival from 650 metres away has not arrived. The distance is not a matter of
 336→degree — the fee either rests on a genuine arrival or it does not.
 337→
 338→### NS-4 — Driver no-show: the rider owes nothing [PEER-DERIVED]
 339→
 340→Where the driver never arrived, or arrived so late that the rider had already cancelled, the
 341→rider is **not** charged and any fee taken is refunded in full. Ryde publishes no rider-facing
 342→rule for this case; Grab does: "Cancellation fees are waived if your driver does not arrive within
 343→3 minutes after the first-shown estimated time of arrival", and TADA auto-cancels at no charge
 344→where the driver is not on the way.
 345→
 346→Where the records additionally suggest the non-arrival was deliberate — the driver stationary and
 347→distant, no contact attempt, a pattern in the profile — the finding is recorded under GEN-7 for
 348→the platform's fraud process. This policy still only decides the money.
 349→
 350→### NS-5 — Waiting time fee [RYDE-ACTUAL]
 351→
 352→Distinct from cancellation: where the driver pressed "I'm Here", waited more than 3 minutes, **and
 353→the trip went ahead**, a waiting time fee of SGD 5.00 is chargeable at the end of the trip. The
 354→same arrival test in NS-3 applies: a waiting fee earned from the wrong location is not earned.
 355→
 356→### NS-6 — Contested no-show with both parties asserting [SYNTHESISED]
 357→
 358→Where the driver marked a no-show and the rider asserts the driver was absent
 359→(`cancellation.driver_marked_no_show` true and `cancellation.rider_claims_driver_absent` true),
 360→the platform's own telemetry decides it, in this order: the driver's recorded position at arrival
 361→(NS-3), then the wait duration (NS-2), then the chat log's contemporaneous content.
 362→
 363→If the telemetry settles it, rule and explain which field decided. If the position is unrecorded
 364→and the wait is the only evidence, the dispute escalates under ESC-3: a straight word-against-word
 365→conflict on a fee is not something to decide on the balance of personalities.
 366→
 367→### NS-7 — Advance bookings [RYDE-ACTUAL]
 368→
 369→For advance trips, cancellations more than 15 minutes before the scheduled time are free. Inside
 370→that window the cancellation fee applies, except that a booking accepted less than 15 minutes
 371→before the scheduled time carries a 3-minute grace period from acceptance.
 372→
 373→The driver-side tests in NS-2 through NS-4 apply unchanged to advance bookings.
 374→
 375→---
 376→
 377→## 5. Escalation to human review
 378→
 379→Escalation is a correct outcome, not a failure. A wrong ruling delivered confidently costs more
 380→than a slow one.
 381→
 382→### ESC-1 — Out of scope [SYNTHESISED]
 383→
 384→Any dispute outside the two categories in GEN-1 goes to human review without an agent ruling. The
 385→parties receive a neutral acknowledgement that the matter has been passed to the support team.
 386→
 387→### ESC-2 — Missing decisive evidence [SYNTHESISED]
 388→
 389→Where a pack field the applicable rule depends on is `null`, and no alternative rule reaches the
 390→question, the dispute escalates. Specifically: a route-deviation claim without the distances
 391→required by EV-1, or a no-show claim without the timestamps required by EV-2.
 392→
 393→Do not substitute a plausible figure for a missing one. An estimated deviation is an invented
 394→fact, and a ruling built on it cannot be audited.
 395→
 396→Enforcement (2026-09-23): for route-deviation disputes the Judge withholds any ruling whose
 397→`route.deviation_pct` is null. This gate is enforced in code, beside the confidence gate and the
 398→ESC-4 cap, and applies to route cases only — a no-show without a recorded arrival is never caught,
 399→because there the absence is itself the evidence (NS-4).
 400→
 401→### ESC-3 — Irreconcilable accounts [SYNTHESISED]
 402→
 403→Where the two sides assert incompatible facts and the telemetry does not settle which is right,
 404→the dispute escalates with both cases and the full Evidence Pack attached. NS-6 is the common
 405→instance.
 406→
 407→### ESC-4 — Amount above the autonomous cap [SYNTHESISED]
 408→
 409→Where the remedy under consideration exceeds **SGD 50.00**, the ruling is prepared but not issued:
 410→it goes to a human reviewer as a recommendation. Automated systems should not move large sums
 411→without a person in the loop, and the cap is deliberately low relative to the fees in scope.
 412→
 413→### ESC-5 — Low confidence [SYNTHESISED]
 414→
 415→Where the Judge's own confidence in the ruling falls below the configured threshold, the ruling is
 416→withheld regardless of its content and the case goes to human review with the candidate ruling
 417→attached. The parties see only a neutral notice that the case is still under review.
 418→
 419→Confidence is an honest estimate that the ruling is the one the policy and the evidence support.
 420→It is not a measure of how strongly the Judge feels, and it is not to be inflated to clear the
 421→threshold or deflated to avoid deciding. A case that is genuinely clear — the rule fires, the
 422→evidence is complete, neither side's account is in doubt — should carry high confidence and be
 423→decided.
 424→
 425→### ESC-6 — What the parties are told on escalation [SYNTHESISED]
 426→
 427→An escalated dispute produces a neutral holding message: the case is under review and the party
 428→will be contacted. The parties are **not** told which way the candidate ruling went, what the
 429→confidence score was, or that an automated system was uncertain. A provisional outcome disclosed
 430→and then reversed is worse than a short wait.
 431→
 432→### ESC-7 — Target timelines [PEER-DERIVED]
 433→
 434→Escalated disputes should be acknowledged within **3 working days** and resolved within **21
 435→working days**. Neither Ryde nor Grab nor TADA publishes a rider-side resolution SLA for fare
 436→disputes; these figures are the CaseTrust-LTA accreditation standard for the car-sharing
 437→industry, which is the nearest published Singapore benchmark ("Operators must acknowledge receipt
 438→of complaints within three working days and address the dispute within 21 working days").
 439→
 440→---
 441→
 442→## 6. Outcomes
 443→
 444→A ruling states one of three actions.
 445→
 446→**refund** — money returns to the rider: a fee refunded under Section 4, or a fare overcharge
 447→returned under Section 3. The amount and the form of remedy (GEN-5) are stated.
 448→
 449→**compensation** — money moves to the driver. In scope here only where a fee was correctly earned
 450→and had been reversed, or where a rider's conduct cost the driver a fee they were entitled to.
 451→
 452→**no action** — the charge stands, or the deviation carried no fare consequence. This is a
 453→ruling like any other and requires the same explanation and the same confidence. A system that
 454→can only find for the complainant is not adjudicating.
 455→
 456→Every ruling cites the rule IDs it rests on and the Evidence Pack fields that satisfied them, and
 457→explains the reasoning in language both parties can read.
 458→

{"content":"# Architecture

This document explains the system to someone who has read the README and has five minutes.
Every claim here describes the code as it stands; nothing is planned or partial except where
the Limits section says so plainly.

## Overview

Ryde is a multi-agent dispute resolution system for ride-hailing: a party files a dispute
through a web intake form, and the system resolves the two categories it handles — route
deviation and no-show charge — end to end. Three agents do the work: a Rider Advocate and a
Driver Advocate each build their side's case from the evidence, and a Judge weighs both
cases, applies company policy and issues a ruling with a confidence score. Every number the
agents argue from comes from a deterministic Evidence Pack computed in Python before any
model is called; agents cite pack fields by reference and are forbidden from doing their own
arithmetic. The decisions that must never depend on a model's obedience — the confidence
threshold, the SGD 50 autonomous cap, the requirement that a route ruling rest on a measured
deviation, the one-round follow-up limit, and the routing of out-of-scope categories to
human review — are enforced in Python code, not asked of the model in a prompt. The system
has two surfaces: an operator console that shows the full case file and the agent-to-agent
traffic, and a party page where the filing party submits the form and reads only what they
are allowed to read.

## Diagram

The whole system on one page. The party-facing flow runs top to bottom, the two swappable
inputs (the policy document and the dataset pack) enter from the side, and every step of a
run lands in the event log that the operator console reads.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Rider intake form"] --> B["Server"]
    PACK["Dataset pack"] --> A
    B --> C{"Category in scope?"}
    C -- "Out of scope" --> H["Human review"]
    C -- "Route deviation or no-show" --> E["Evidence Pack"]
    POL["Policy document"] --> RA["Rider Advocate"]
    POL --> DA["Driver Advocate"]
    POL --> J["Judge"]
    E --> RA
    E --> DA
    RA --> S{"Questions for the party?"}
    DA --> S
    S -- "Yes, first round" --> O4["Needs info"]
    O4 --> PA["Party answers follow-ups"]
    PA -- "Fresh run with the answers" --> B
    S -- "No" --> J
    J --> G{"Gates pass? Confidence, cap, measured deviation"}
    G -- "Yes" --> O1["Ruled"]
    G -- "No" --> O2["Withheld"]
    B -. "Every step emits an event" .-> L["Event log"]
    J -.-> L
    L --> K["Operator console"]
```

## Components

| Component | File(s) | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| Pipeline | `app/pipeline.py` | Runs one dispute end to end, moves the case between agents, records every step |
| Dispute record and routing | `app/dispute.py` | Parses the two record shapes, normalises categories, routes out-of-scope filings away |
| Evidence layer | `app/evidence/compute.py` | Computes the Evidence Pack by plain arithmetic; a missing input becomes a null with a note, never a guess |
| Agent scaffolding | `app/agents/base.py` | Shared prompts, the LLM call, and citation validation against the pack and the policy |
| Rider Advocate | `app/agents/rider_advocate.py` | Argues the rider's side from the pack and the policy |
| Driver Advocate | `app/agents/driver_advocate.py` | Argues the driver's side from the pack and the policy |
| Judge | `app/agents/judge.py` | Weighs both cases, issues one ruling, withholds it behind the gates |
| Event log | `app/events.py` | The append-only record of who said what to whom, with full payloads on disk |
| Output contracts | `app/schemas.py` | The typed shapes agents must produce; builds the party-facing decision message |
| Policy loader | `app/policy.py` | Reads the policy document, extracts rule IDs, fails loudly when it is missing |
| Mock LLM | `app/llm/mock.py` | Deterministic stand-in provider; every string it returns is `MOCK`-prefixed |
| Tencent adapter | `app/llm/tencent.py` | The real provider over HTTP; the endpoint is not pinned yet, so it is never called |
| HTTP server | `app/server.py` | The intake API, the party view allowlist, and static files for both pages |
| Command-line runner | `app/cli.py` | Runs one dispute from the terminal and prints the event strip |
| Runtime configuration | `app/config.json` | Confidence threshold, autonomous cap, default dataset pack, provider settings |
| Operator console | `ui/app.js` | Renders the case file: grievance, evidence, both claims, resolution, event strip |
| Party page | `ui/party/party.js` | The intake form and the outcome view the filing party sees |
| Policy document | `docs/policy.md` | The rule set the agents cite, with per-rule provenance |

## Lifecycle of a dispute

`run_dispute` in `app/pipeline.py` walks one dispute through these steps, in this order,
emitting an event at each:

1. `run.started` — the system records the dispute id, category, LLM provider, confidence
   threshold and the policy rule IDs in force.
2. `dispute.filed` — the raw intake-form submission is logged exactly as it arrived.
3. **Routing.** If the category is outside the two handled ones, the run emits
   `dispute.routed_to_human_review`, then `party.notified` with the neutral support message,
   then `run.completed` — and no agent runs at all.
4. `evidence.pack_built` — the Evidence Pack is computed in Python, before any LLM call,
   and offered to the agents as the only source of numbers.
5. `case.assigned` — once to each advocate.
6. Each advocate runs and emits `advocate.case_submitted` to the Judge with its case. When
   an advocate needs more from the filing party, it also emits
   `advocate.follow_up_requested` — but only in the first round, and only for questions
   that pass the party-safety check.
7. **Stop and ask.** If the advocates produced questions and the dispute does not already
   carry the party's answers, the run stops before the Judge: `party.notified` carries the
   questions, then `run.completed` records the `needs_info` outcome. The party's answers
   start a fresh run, which is guaranteed to reach the Judge.
8. `judge.deliberation_started` — both cases are handed to the Judge together.
9. The Judge rules: `judge.ruling_issued` when every gate passes, or
   `judge.ruling_withheld` when one fails — the candidate ruling is recorded either way.
10. `party.notified` — the message the parties actually receive, as opposed to what was
    decided internally.
11. `run.completed` — the outcome is recorded and the case file is written.

## The four outcomes

| Outcome | When it happens | Did the Judge run? | Party page shows |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ruled` | The Judge issued a ruling and every gate passed | Yes | `decided` |
| `withheld` | A gate stopped the ruling: confidence below threshold, amount above the cap, or an unmeasured deviation on a route case | Yes — the candidate is recorded for a human reviewer, never delivered | `under_review` |
| `human_review` | The category is outside the two the agents handle | No — routed away before any agent | `passed_to_support` |
| `needs_info` | The advocates asked targeted follow-up questions in the first round | No — the run stops before the Judge | `needs_info` |

## Gates enforced in code

Five gates stand between a filing and a ruling, and each is a Python conditional, not a
prompt instruction:

| Gate | File | Condition as written in code |
|---|---|---|
| Confidence threshold | `app/agents/judge.py` | `ruling.confidence < confidence_threshold` — the threshold is 0.65, read from `app/config.json` |
| ESC-4, the autonomous cap | `app/agents/judge.py` | A money ruling whose `recommended_amount_sgd` exceeds the cap is withheld; the cap is SGD 50 from `app/config.json` |
| ESC-2, unmeasured deviation | `app/agents/judge.py` | On a route-deviation case, `pack.route.deviation_pct is null` withholds the ruling — a route ruling must name the deviation it rests on |
| One-round follow-up limit | `app/pipeline.py` | `if questions and not dispute.follow_up_answers` — a dispute is asked at most once; with answers present the Judge always runs and fresh questions are recorded but not sent |
| Out-of-scope routing | `app/pipeline.py` | `if not dispute.is_agent_handled` — anything outside route deviation and no-show charge goes to human review before any agent runs; an unrecognised category normalises to "other" in `app/dispute.py` |

Why in code? Because a prompt is a request — a model can misread it, and there is no
recourse when it does. Code is a guarantee: the branch either runs or it does not, and the
event log shows which. ESC-4 in particular moves money, so it must not depend on the LLM
having read its instructions carefully.

## Observability

Every run writes three things under `runs/<run_id>/`:

- `events.jsonl` — one JSON line per event, append-only, never rewritten: who sent what to
  whom, when, with a one-line summary.
- `payloads/` — the full payload behind each event, named by sequence number and event
  type, so the strip stays readable and the detail stays one click away.
- `case_file.json` — the assembled record: what was claimed, the evidence pack, both
  advocate cases, the resolution, and the event strip. Self-contained, so one file tells
  the whole story of one run.

The operator console (`ui/app.js`) renders the case file: the event strip shows one row per
event — sequence, time, sender to recipient, summary — and expanding a row opens the full
payload from the run directory attached in the browser. Payload references are sanitised, so
a console loaded with a hostile file can be pointed at nothing outside the run. The
command-line runner prints the same strip to the terminal.

## What the parties see

`party_view` in `app/server.py` is an allowlist that fails closed. The party page is handed
exactly five keys — run id, dispute id, status, message, questions — and any malformed case
file degrades to the neutral under-review message with no questions. A withheld ruling's
amount and the Judge's confidence are structurally absent from everything the party is
sent, not merely unrendered. `party_message_for_ruling` in `app/schemas.py` composes the
decision message in code from structured fields — the action, the amount, and the plain
titles of the policy rules cited — and the Judge's explanation never crosses this boundary:
it stays in the operator console. Every non-decision status shows a canonical constant
message, whatever a stale or planted case file might say. The word check on questions is a
backstop, not the protection: the protection is that party-facing text is composed in code
from structured fields, so there is nothing unsafe for the check to find.

## Policy and dataset packs

`docs/policy.md` is data, not code: rules with IDs (GEN, EV, RD, NS, ESC families),
machine-checkable preconditions written against pack fields, and per-rule provenance
stating whether a rule comes from Ryde's own published policy, a comparable operator, or
the project team. The pipeline reads it at the path in `app/config.json`; a different
policy document drops in with no code change, and agents may cite only IDs the loader
found in it.

Two dataset packs live under `data/packs/`: `organiser-style-v1` — the default in
`app/config.json` — which holds the corpus in the organisers' record shape, including their
own DISP-002 verbatim; and `ryde-synth-v1`, the same 17 cases in this project's own record
shape. Swapping corpora is a directory copy, never a code change. Each pack carries a
`ground-truth.json` of expected outcomes, kept out of what the agents see: the agents get
the dispute record, the evidence pack and the policy — never the answer — so replayed-run
consistency can be measured honestly.

## LLM provider

Agent logic never talks to a vendor SDK. Every agent builds a request and calls one seam:
the `LLMClient` interface in `app/llm/`, a single `complete` method whose response carries
the text plus provenance (provider, model, usage, finish reason). Two adapters implement
it. The mock provider, `app/llm/mock.py`, returns deterministic contract-shaped responses,
so the full pipeline runs with no API key and the same dispute always produces the same
case file; every string it returns carries a `MOCK` prefix, so a mock run can never be
mistaken for a real ruling. The Tencent adapter, `app/llm/tencent.py`, implements the same
interface over HTTP — and is honest about its status: the concrete service, endpoint, auth
scheme and payload shape are not pinned yet, the configuration still carries placeholder
values, and the adapter fails loudly rather than silently falling back to the mock. To be
plain: the Tencent endpoint has not been called. Every run to date is a mock run, a
plumbing demonstration rather than a model judgement.

## Limits

What the system does not do yet, stated plainly:

- **No real LLM calls.** The mock provider answers every agent. Nothing here has reasoned
  about a dispute; the machinery around the reasoning is what is built and tested.
- **Two categories only.** Route deviation and no-show charge. Property damage and safety
  incidents route to human review by design.
- **The driver-side form is not built.** The party page files as the rider only; the
  pipeline itself accepts driver-filed disputes, but no web form offers it yet.
- **The word check is incomplete by design.** It is a keyword backstop over a banned
  vocabulary, not a semantic guarantee. The boundary holds because of the structure around
  it — the allowlist, the code-built messages, the canonical constants — not because the
  word list is clever.

## The challenge

Ride-hailing platforms process thousands of dispute tickets daily: fare disputes, route deviations,
property damage, safety incidents, no-show charges. They are subjective, emotionally charged, and
currently resolved by humans reviewing GPS telemetry, chat logs, payment records and company policy
by hand. The result is slow, expensive and inconsistent.

The task is an autonomous multi-agent system that gathers evidence, builds both sides' cases, applies
company policy and issues a fair ruling with a confidence score and a plain-language explanation.

## Planned architecture

Three core agents, all MVP-required:

| Agent | Role |
|---|---|
| **Rider Advocate** | Gathers rider-side evidence, argues the rider's case from policy |
| **Driver Advocate** | Gathers driver-side evidence, argues the driver's case from policy |
| **Judge** | Weighs both cases, applies policy, rules, and explains the reasoning with a confidence score |

Inter-agent communication must be **observable** — a judge needs to see how the agents exchange
information and build their cases. That surface is a required deliverable, not a nice-to-have.

## Documents

- [`docs/statement-extract.md`](docs/statement-extract.md) — the challenge statement, verbatim
- `docs/architecture.md` — architecture diagram and system description (required deliverable, to come)
- [`docs/policy.md`](docs/policy.md) — the policy rule set the Judge applies, with per-rule provenance
- [`docs/dataset.md`](docs/dataset.md) — the labelled corpus, its provenance and its limitations
- [`docs/evidence-plan.md`](docs/evidence-plan.md) — development-process evidence rules
- [`CODEBUDDY.md`](CODEBUDDY.md) — builder's entry point and project memory

## Development tooling

Built with Tencent Cloud **CodeBuddy**. The competition mandates proof of product usage, so
development happens in the tool and evidence is captured as it occurs.

## Run

No dependencies and no API key needed for the skeleton: it runs on a stock Python 3.9+ with the
standard library only, using a deterministic mock in place of the LLM.

```bash

python3 -m app.cli --pack ryde-synth-v1 --dispute RD-0101
python3 -m app.cli --pack organiser-style-v1 --dispute DISP-002
```

`--dispute` takes either a dispute id inside the selected pack or a path to a record file
(`python3 -m app.cli --dispute data/packs/ryde-synth-v1/disputes/RD-0101.json`). The pack
defaults to `dataset_pack` in `app/config.json`; `--pack` overrides it for one run.

That prints the agent-to-agent event strip and the ruling, and writes the run's artifacts to
`runs/<run_id>/`: `events.jsonl` (the observable traffic), `payloads/*.json` (the full payload
behind each event) and `case_file.json` (evidence, both claims, resolution).

The corpus lives in two swappable packs under `data/packs/`: `ryde-synth-v1` (our 17 labelled
cases, our record shape) and `organiser-style-v1` (the same 17 cases as twins in the organisers'
shape, plus the organisers' own `DISP-002` verbatim). `RD-0103` is a deviation too small to
matter, `NS-0203` is a driver who marked arrival 885 m from the pickup point, `RD-0109` is a
remedy above the autonomous cap that the system refuses to issue on its own, and `OS-0301` is an
out-of-scope filing routed to human review without an LLM call. `docs/dataset.md` maps each case
to what it tests; `<pack>/ground-truth.json` holds the expected outcomes, deliberately kept out
of the records the agents see.

Two gates stand between a ruling and the parties, and **both are enforced in Python, not asked of
the model in a prompt**: the confidence threshold and ESC-4's SGD 50 autonomous cap. Try them:


Tencent endpoint is not pinned yet (see the TODO block in `app/llm/tencent.py`) — a mock run is a
plumbing demonstration, never a real ruling.

The demo walkthrough and its recording land once the case-file UI and the real LLM call are in.

1→# Ryde — Multi-Agent Autonomous Dispute Resolution
   2→
   3→Entry for the **Tencent Cloud "AI CAN DO IT" Hackathon Singapore 2026**, Digital Native track
   4→(the Ryde challenge statement, section 5 of the organisers' document).
   5→
   6→**Status: building (since 2026-09-21).** The scope
   7→is ruled: a two-category MVP (route deviation + no-show charge) with three agents, a
   8→deterministic evidence layer, and an observable case-file view. The challenge statement is in
   9→[`docs/statement-extract.md`](docs/statement-extract.md); the builder's contract is in
  10→[`CODEBUDDY.md`](CODEBUDDY.md).
  11→
  12→## The challenge
  13→
  14→Ride-hailing platforms process thousands of dispute tickets daily: fare disputes, route deviations,
  15→property damage, safety incidents, no-show charges. They are subjective, emotionally charged, and
  16→currently resolved by humans reviewing GPS telemetry, chat logs, payment records and company policy
  17→by hand. The result is slow, expensive and inconsistent.
  18→
  19→The task is an autonomous multi-agent system that gathers evidence, builds both sides' cases, applies
  20→company policy and issues a fair ruling with a confidence score and a plain-language explanation.
  21→
  22→## Planned architecture
  23→
  24→Three core agents, all MVP-required:
  25→
  26→| Agent | Role |
  27→|---|---|
  28→| **Rider Advocate** | Gathers rider-side evidence, argues the rider's case from policy |
  29→| **Driver Advocate** | Gathers driver-side evidence, argues the driver's case from policy |
  30→| **Judge** | Weighs both cases, applies policy, rules, and explains the reasoning with a confidence score |
  31→
  32→Inter-agent communication must be **observable** — a judge needs to see how the agents exchange
  33→information and build their cases. That surface is a required deliverable, not a nice-to-have.
  34→
  35→## Documents
  36→
  37→- [`docs/statement-extract.md`](docs/statement-extract.md) — the challenge statement, verbatim
  38→- `docs/architecture.md` — architecture diagram and system description (required deliverable, to come)
  39→- [`docs/policy.md`](docs/policy.md) — the policy rule set the Judge applies, with per-rule provenance
  40→- [`docs/dataset.md`](docs/dataset.md) — the labelled corpus, its provenance and its limitations
  41→- [`docs/evidence-plan.md`](docs/evidence-plan.md) — development-process evidence rules
  42→- [`CODEBUDDY.md`](CODEBUDDY.md) — builder's entry point and project memory
  43→
  44→## Development tooling
  45→
  46→Built with Tencent Cloud **CodeBuddy**. The competition mandates proof of product usage, so
  47→development happens in the tool and evidence is captured as it occurs.
  48→
  49→## Run
  50→
  51→No dependencies and no API key needed for the skeleton: it runs on a stock Python 3.9+ with the
  52→standard library only, using a deterministic mock in place of the LLM.
  53→
  54→```bash
  55→python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -t .        # 225 tests
  56→python3 -m app.cli --pack ryde-synth-v1 --dispute RD-0101
  57→python3 -m app.cli --pack organiser-style-v1 --dispute DISP-002
  58→```
  59→
  60→`--dispute` takes either a dispute id inside the selected pack or a path to a record file
  61→(`python3 -m app.cli --dispute data/packs/ryde-synth-v1/disputes/RD-0101.json`). The pack
  62→defaults to `dataset_pack` in `app/config.json`; `--pack` overrides it for one run.
  63→
  64→That prints the agent-to-agent event strip and the ruling, and writes the run's artifacts to
  65→`runs/<run_id>/`: `events.jsonl` (the observable traffic), `payloads/*.json` (the full payload
  66→behind each event) and `case_file.json` (evidence, both claims, resolution).
  67→
  68→The corpus lives in two swappable packs under `data/packs/`: `ryde-synth-v1` (our 17 labelled
  69→cases, our record shape) and `organiser-style-v1` (the same 17 cases as twins in the organisers'
  70→shape, plus the organisers' own `DISP-002` verbatim). `RD-0103` is a deviation too small to
  71→matter, `NS-0203` is a driver who marked arrival 885 m from the pickup point, `RD-0109` is a
  72→remedy above the autonomous cap that the system refuses to issue on its own, and `OS-0301` is an
  73→out-of-scope filing routed to human review without an LLM call. `docs/dataset.md` maps each case
  74→to what it tests; `<pack>/ground-truth.json` holds the expected outcomes, deliberately kept out
  75→of the records the agents see.
  76→
  77→Two gates stand between a ruling and the parties, and **both are enforced in Python, not asked of
  78→the model in a prompt**: the confidence threshold and ESC-4's SGD 50 autonomous cap. Try them:
  79→
  80→```bash
  81→python3 -m app.cli --pack ryde-synth-v1 --dispute RD-0109   # withheld: above the cap
  82→```
  83→
  84→**One caveat while the build is in progress.** Every mock string is prefixed `MOCK`, because the
  85→Tencent endpoint is not pinned yet (see the TODO block in `app/llm/tencent.py`) — a mock run is a
  86→plumbing demonstration, never a real ruling.
  87→
  88→The demo walkthrough and its recording land once the case-file UI and the real LLM call are in.
  89→

1→# Architecture
   2→
   3→This document explains the system to someone who has read the README and has five minutes.
   4→Every claim here describes the code as it stands; nothing is planned or partial except where
   5→the Limits section says so plainly.
   6→
   7→## Overview
   8→
   9→Ryde is a multi-agent dispute resolution system for ride-hailing: a party files a dispute
  10→through a web intake form, and the system resolves the two categories it handles — route
  11→deviation and no-show charge — end to end. Three agents do the work: a Rider Advocate and a
  12→Driver Advocate each build their side's case from the evidence, and a Judge weighs both
  13→cases, applies company policy and issues a ruling with a confidence score. Every number the
  14→agents argue from comes from a deterministic Evidence Pack computed in Python before any
  15→model is called; agents cite pack fields by reference and are forbidden from doing their own
  16→arithmetic. The decisions that must never depend on a model's obedience — the confidence
  17→threshold, the SGD 50 autonomous cap, the requirement that a route ruling rest on a measured
  18→deviation, the one-round follow-up limit, and the routing of out-of-scope categories to
  19→human review — are enforced in Python code, not asked of the model in a prompt. The system
  20→has two surfaces: an operator console that shows the full case file and the agent-to-agent
  21→traffic, and a party page where the filing party submits the form and reads only what they
  22→are allowed to read.
  23→
  24→## Diagram
  25→
  26→The whole system on one page. The party-facing flow runs top to bottom, the two swappable
  27→inputs (the policy document and the dataset pack) enter from the side, and every step of a
  28→run lands in the event log that the operator console reads.
  29→
  30→```mermaid
  31→flowchart TD
  32→    A["Rider intake form"] --> B["Server"]
  33→    PACK["Dataset pack"] --> A
  34→    B --> C{"Category in scope?"}
  35→    C -- "Out of scope" --> H["Human review"]
  36→    C -- "Route deviation or no-show" --> E["Evidence Pack"]
  37→    POL["Policy document"] --> RA["Rider Advocate"]
  38→    POL --> DA["Driver Advocate"]
  39→    POL --> J["Judge"]
  40→    E --> RA
  41→    E --> DA
  42→    RA --> S{"Questions for the party?"}
  43→    DA --> S
  44→    S -- "Yes, first round" --> O4["Needs info"]
  45→    O4 --> PA["Party answers follow-ups"]
  46→    PA -- "Fresh run with the answers" --> B
  47→    S -- "No" --> J
  48→    J --> G{"Gates pass? Confidence, cap, measured deviation"}
  49→    G -- "Yes" --> O1["Ruled"]
  50→    G -- "No" --> O2["Withheld"]
  51→    B -. "Every step emits an event" .-> L["Event log"]
  52→    J -.-> L
  53→    L --> K["Operator console"]
  54→```
  55→
  56→## Components
  57→
  58→| Component | File(s) | Responsibility |
  59→|---|---|---|
  60→| Pipeline | `app/pipeline.py` | Runs one dispute end to end, moves the case between agents, records every step |
  61→| Dispute record and routing | `app/dispute.py` | Parses the two record shapes, normalises categories, routes out-of-scope filings away |
  62→| Evidence layer | `app/evidence/compute.py` | Computes the Evidence Pack by plain arithmetic; a missing input becomes a null with a note, never a guess |
  63→| Agent scaffolding | `app/agents/base.py` | Shared prompts, the LLM call, and citation validation against the pack and the policy |
  64→| Rider Advocate | `app/agents/rider_advocate.py` | Argues the rider's side from the pack and the policy |
  65→| Driver Advocate | `app/agents/driver_advocate.py` | Argues the driver's side from the pack and the policy |
  66→| Judge | `app/agents/judge.py` | Weighs both cases, issues one ruling, withholds it behind the gates |
  67→| Event log | `app/events.py` | The append-only record of who said what to whom, with full payloads on disk |
  68→| Output contracts | `app/schemas.py` | The typed shapes agents must produce; builds the party-facing decision message |
  69→| Policy loader | `app/policy.py` | Reads the policy document, extracts rule IDs, fails loudly when it is missing |
  70→| Mock LLM | `app/llm/mock.py` | Deterministic stand-in provider; every string it returns is `MOCK`-prefixed |
  71→| Tencent adapter | `app/llm/tencent.py` | The real provider over HTTP; the endpoint is not pinned yet, so it is never called |
  72→| HTTP server | `app/server.py` | The intake API, the party view allowlist, and static files for both pages |
  73→| Command-line runner | `app/cli.py` | Runs one dispute from the terminal and prints the event strip |
  74→| Runtime configuration | `app/config.json` | Confidence threshold, autonomous cap, default dataset pack, provider settings |
  75→| Operator console | `ui/app.js` | Renders the case file: grievance, evidence, both claims, resolution, event strip |
  76→| Party page | `ui/party/party.js` | The intake form and the outcome view the filing party sees |
  77→| Policy document | `docs/policy.md` | The rule set the agents cite, with per-rule provenance |
  78→
  79→## Lifecycle of a dispute
  80→
  81→`run_dispute` in `app/pipeline.py` walks one dispute through these steps, in this order,
  82→emitting an event at each:
  83→
  84→1. `run.started` — the system records the dispute id, category, LLM provider, confidence
  85→   threshold and the policy rule IDs in force.
  86→2. `dispute.filed` — the raw intake-form submission is logged exactly as it arrived.
  87→3. **Routing.** If the category is outside the two handled ones, the run emits
  88→   `dispute.routed_to_human_review`, then `party.notified` with the neutral support message,
  89→   then `run.completed` — and no agent runs at all.
  90→4. `evidence.pack_built` — the Evidence Pack is computed in Python, before any LLM call,
  91→   and offered to the agents as the only source of numbers.
  92→5. `case.assigned` — once to each advocate.
  93→6. Each advocate runs and emits `advocate.case_submitted` to the Judge with its case. When
  94→   an advocate needs more from the filing party, it also emits
  95→   `advocate.follow_up_requested` — but only in the first round, and only for questions
  96→   that pass the party-safety check.
  97→7. **Stop and ask.** If the advocates produced questions and the dispute does not already
  98→   carry the party's answers, the run stops before the Judge: `party.notified` carries the
  99→   questions, then `run.completed` records the `needs_info` outcome. The party's answers
 100→   start a fresh run, which is guaranteed to reach the Judge.
 101→8. `judge.deliberation_started` — both cases are handed to the Judge together.
 102→9. The Judge rules: `judge.ruling_issued` when every gate passes, or
 103→   `judge.ruling_withheld` when one fails — the candidate ruling is recorded either way.
 104→10. `party.notified` — the message the parties actually receive, as opposed to what was
 105→    decided internally.
 106→11. `run.completed` — the outcome is recorded and the case file is written.
 107→
 108→## The four outcomes
 109→
 110→| Outcome | When it happens | Did the Judge run? | Party page shows |
 111→|---|---|---|---|
 112→| `ruled` | The Judge issued a ruling and every gate passed | Yes | `decided` |
 113→| `withheld` | A gate stopped the ruling: confidence below threshold, amount above the cap, or an unmeasured deviation on a route case | Yes — the candidate is recorded for a human reviewer, never delivered | `under_review` |
 114→| `human_review` | The category is outside the two the agents handle | No — routed away before any agent | `passed_to_support` |
 115→| `needs_info` | The advocates asked targeted follow-up questions in the first round | No — the run stops before the Judge | `needs_info` |
 116→
 117→## Gates enforced in code
 118→
 119→Five gates stand between a filing and a ruling, and each is a Python conditional, not a
 120→prompt instruction:
 121→
 122→| Gate | File | Condition as written in code |
 123→|---|---|---|
 124→| Confidence threshold | `app/agents/judge.py` | `ruling.confidence < confidence_threshold` — the threshold is 0.65, read from `app/config.json` |
 125→| ESC-4, the autonomous cap | `app/agents/judge.py` | A money ruling whose `recommended_amount_sgd` exceeds the cap is withheld; the cap is SGD 50 from `app/config.json` |
 126→| ESC-2, unmeasured deviation | `app/agents/judge.py` | On a route-deviation case, `pack.route.deviation_pct is null` withholds the ruling — a route ruling must name the deviation it rests on |
 127→| One-round follow-up limit | `app/pipeline.py` | `if questions and not dispute.follow_up_answers` — a dispute is asked at most once; with answers present the Judge always runs and fresh questions are recorded but not sent |
 128→| Out-of-scope routing | `app/pipeline.py` | `if not dispute.is_agent_handled` — anything outside route deviation and no-show charge goes to human review before any agent runs; an unrecognised category normalises to "other" in `app/dispute.py` |
 129→
 130→Why in code? Because a prompt is a request — a model can misread it, and there is no
 131→recourse when it does. Code is a guarantee: the branch either runs or it does not, and the
 132→event log shows which. ESC-4 in particular moves money, so it must not depend on the LLM
 133→having read its instructions carefully.
 134→
 135→## Observability
 136→
 137→Every run writes three things under `runs/<run_id>/`:
 138→
 139→- `events.jsonl` — one JSON line per event, append-only, never rewritten: who sent what to
 140→  whom, when, with a one-line summary.
 141→- `payloads/` — the full payload behind each event, named by sequence number and event
 142→  type, so the strip stays readable and the detail stays one click away.
 143→- `case_file.json` — the assembled record: what was claimed, the evidence pack, both
 144→  advocate cases, the resolution, and the event strip. Self-contained, so one file tells
 145→  the whole story of one run.
 146→
 147→The operator console (`ui/app.js`) renders the case file: the event strip shows one row per
 148→event — sequence, time, sender to recipient, summary — and expanding a row opens the full
 149→payload from the run directory attached in the browser. Payload references are sanitised, so
 150→a console loaded with a hostile file can be pointed at nothing outside the run. The
 151→command-line runner prints the same strip to the terminal.
 152→
 153→## What the parties see
 154→
 155→`party_view` in `app/server.py` is an allowlist that fails closed. The party page is handed
 156→exactly five keys — run id, dispute id, status, message, questions — and any malformed case
 157→file degrades to the neutral under-review message with no questions. A withheld ruling's
 158→amount and the Judge's confidence are structurally absent from everything the party is
 159→sent, not merely unrendered. `party_message_for_ruling` in `app/schemas.py` composes the
 160→decision message in code from structured fields — the action, the amount, and the plain
 161→titles of the policy rules cited — and the Judge's explanation never crosses this boundary:
 162→it stays in the operator console. Every non-decision status shows a canonical constant
 163→message, whatever a stale or planted case file might say. The word check on questions is a
 164→backstop, not the protection: the protection is that party-facing text is composed in code
 165→from structured fields, so there is nothing unsafe for the check to find.
 166→
 167→## Policy and dataset packs
 168→
 169→`docs/policy.md` is data, not code: rules with IDs (GEN, EV, RD, NS, ESC families),
 170→machine-checkable preconditions written against pack fields, and per-rule provenance
 171→stating whether a rule comes from Ryde's own published policy, a comparable operator, or
 172→the project team. The pipeline reads it at the path in `app/config.json`; a different
 173→policy document drops in with no code change, and agents may cite only IDs the loader
 174→found in it.
 175→
 176→Two dataset packs live under `data/packs/`: `organiser-style-v1` — the default in
 177→`app/config.json` — which holds the corpus in the organisers' record shape, including their
 178→own DISP-002 verbatim; and `ryde-synth-v1`, the same 17 cases in this project's own record
 179→shape. Swapping corpora is a directory copy, never a code change. Each pack carries a
 180→`ground-truth.json` of expected outcomes, kept out of what the agents see: the agents get
 181→the dispute record, the evidence pack and the policy — never the answer — so replayed-run
 182→consistency can be measured honestly.
 183→
 184→## LLM provider
 185→
 186→Agent logic never talks to a vendor SDK. Every agent builds a request and calls one seam:
 187→the `LLMClient` interface in `app/llm/`, a single `complete` method whose response carries
 188→the text plus provenance (provider, model, usage, finish reason). Two adapters implement
 189→it. The mock provider, `app/llm/mock.py`, returns deterministic contract-shaped responses,
 190→so the full pipeline runs with no API key and the same dispute always produces the same
 191→case file; every string it returns carries a `MOCK` prefix, so a mock run can never be
 192→mistaken for a real ruling. The Tencent adapter, `app/llm/tencent.py`, implements the same
 193→interface over HTTP — and is honest about its status: the concrete service, endpoint, auth
 194→scheme and payload shape are not pinned yet, the configuration still carries placeholder
 195→values, and the adapter fails loudly rather than silently falling back to the mock. To be
 196→plain: the Tencent endpoint has not been called. Every run to date is a mock run, a
 197→plumbing demonstration rather than a model judgement.
 198→
 199→## Limits
 200→
 201→What the system does not do yet, stated plainly:
 202→
 203→- **No real LLM calls.** The mock provider answers every agent. Nothing here has reasoned
 204→  about a dispute; the machinery around the reasoning is what is built and tested.
 205→- **Two categories only.** Route deviation and no-show charge. Property damage and safety
 206→  incidents route to human review by design.
 207→- **The driver-side form is not built.** The party page files as the rider only; the
 208→  pipeline itself accepts driver-filed disputes, but no web form offers it yet.
 209→- **The word check is incomplete by design.** It is a keyword backstop over a banned
 210→  vocabulary, not a semantic guarantee. The boundary holds because of the structure around
 211→  it — the allowlist, the code-built messages, the canonical constants — not because the
 212→  word list is clever.
 213→

1→# Ryde — Multi-Agent Autonomous Dispute Resolution
   2→
   3→Entry for the **Tencent Cloud "AI CAN DO IT" Hackathon Singapore 2026**, Digital Native track
   4→(the Ryde challenge statement, section 5 of the organisers' document).
   5→
   6→**Status: building (since 2026-09-21).** The scope
   7→is ruled: a two-category MVP (route deviation + no-show charge) with three agents, a
   8→deterministic evidence layer, and an observable case-file view. The challenge statement is in
   9→[`docs/statement-extract.md`](docs/statement-extract.md); the builder's contract is in
  10→[`CODEBUDDY.md`](CODEBUDDY.md).
  11→
  12→## The challenge
  13→
  14→Ride-hailing platforms process thousands of dispute tickets daily: fare disputes, route deviations,
  15→property damage, safety incidents, no-show charges. They are subjective, emotionally charged, and
  16→currently resolved by humans reviewing GPS telemetry, chat logs, payment records and company policy
  17→by hand. The result is slow, expensive and inconsistent.
  18→
  19→The task is an autonomous multi-agent system that gathers evidence, builds both sides' cases, applies
  20→company policy and issues a fair ruling with a confidence score and a plain-language explanation.
  21→
  22→## Architecture
  23→
  24→Three core agents, all MVP-required:
  25→
  26→| Agent | Role |
  27→|---|---|
  28→| **Rider Advocate** | Gathers rider-side evidence, argues the rider's case from policy |
  29→| **Driver Advocate** | Gathers driver-side evidence, argues the driver's case from policy |
  30→| **Judge** | Weighs both cases, applies policy, rules, and explains the reasoning with a confidence score |
  31→
  32→Inter-agent communication must be **observable** — a judge needs to see how the agents exchange
  33→information and build their cases. That surface is a required deliverable, not a nice-to-have.
  34→
  35→The full walkthrough — components, lifecycle, gates, observability — is in
  36→[`docs/architecture.md`](docs/architecture.md). The system on one page:
  37→
  38→```mermaid
  39→flowchart TD
  40→    A["Rider intake form"] --> B["Server"]
  41→    PACK["Dataset pack"] --> A
  42→    B --> C{"Category in scope?"}
  43→    C -- "Out of scope" --> H["Human review"]
  44→    C -- "Route deviation or no-show" --> E["Evidence Pack"]
  45→    POL["Policy document"] --> RA["Rider Advocate"]
  46→    POL --> DA["Driver Advocate"]
  47→    POL --> J["Judge"]
  48→    E --> RA
  49→    E --> DA
  50→    RA --> S{"Questions for the party?"}
  51→    DA --> S
  52→    S -- "Yes, first round" --> O4["Needs info"]
  53→    O4 --> PA["Party answers follow-ups"]
  54→    PA -- "Fresh run with the answers" --> B
  55→    S -- "No" --> J
  56→    J --> G{"Gates pass? Confidence, cap, measured deviation"}
  57→    G -- "Yes" --> O1["Ruled"]
  58→    G -- "No" --> O2["Withheld"]
  59→    B -. "Every step emits an event" .-> L["Event log"]
  60→    J -.-> L
  61→    L --> K["Operator console"]
  62→```
  63→
  64→## Documents
  65→
  66→- [`docs/statement-extract.md`](docs/statement-extract.md) — the challenge statement, verbatim
  67→- [`docs/architecture.md`](docs/architecture.md) — architecture diagram and system description
  68→- [`docs/policy.md`](docs/policy.md) — the policy rule set the Judge applies, with per-rule provenance
  69→- [`docs/dataset.md`](docs/dataset.md) — the labelled corpus, its provenance and its limitations
  70→- [`docs/evidence-plan.md`](docs/evidence-plan.md) — development-process evidence rules
  71→- [`CODEBUDDY.md`](CODEBUDDY.md) — builder's entry point and project memory
  72→
  73→## Development tooling
  74→
  75→Built with Tencent Cloud **CodeBuddy**. The competition mandates proof of product usage, so
  76→development happens in the tool and evidence is captured as it occurs.
  77→
  78→## Run
  79→
  80→No dependencies and no API key needed for the skeleton: it runs on a stock Python 3.9+ with the
  81→standard library only, using a deterministic mock in place of the LLM.
  82→
  83→```bash
  84→python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -t .
  85→python3 -m app.cli --pack ryde-synth-v1 --dispute RD-0101
  86→python3 -m app.cli --pack organiser-style-v1 --dispute DISP-002
  87→```
  88→
  89→`--dispute` takes either a dispute id inside the selected pack or a path to a record file
  90→(`python3 -m app.cli --dispute data/packs/ryde-synth-v1/disputes/RD-0101.json`). The pack
  91→defaults to `dataset_pack` in `app/config.json`; `--pack` overrides it for one run.
  92→
  93→That prints the agent-to-agent event strip and the ruling, and writes the run's artifacts to
  94→`runs/<run_id>/`: `events.jsonl` (the observable traffic), `payloads/*.json` (the full payload
  95→behind each event) and `case_file.json` (evidence, both claims, resolution).
  96→
  97→The corpus lives in two swappable packs under `data/packs/`: `ryde-synth-v1` (our 17 labelled
  98→cases, our record shape) and `organiser-style-v1` (the same 17 cases as twins in the organisers'
  99→shape, plus the organisers' own `DISP-002` verbatim). `RD-0103` is a deviation too small to
 100→matter, `NS-0203` is a driver who marked arrival 885 m from the pickup point, `RD-0109` is a
 101→remedy above the autonomous cap that the system refuses to issue on its own, and `OS-0301` is an
 102→out-of-scope filing routed to human review without an LLM call. `docs/dataset.md` maps each case
 103→to what it tests; `<pack>/ground-truth.json` holds the expected outcomes, deliberately kept out
 104→of the records the agents see.
 105→
 106→Two gates stand between a ruling and the parties, and **both are enforced in Python, not asked of
 107→the model in a prompt**: the confidence threshold and ESC-4's SGD 50 autonomous cap. Try them:
 108→
 109→```bash
 110→python3 -m app.cli --pack ryde-synth-v1 --dispute RD-0109   # withheld: above the cap
 111→```
 112→
 113→**One caveat while the build is in progress.** Every mock string is prefixed `MOCK`, because the
 114→Tencent endpoint is not pinned yet (see the TODO block in `app/llm/tencent.py`) — a mock run is a
 115→plumbing demonstration, never a real ruling.
 116→
 117→The demo walkthrough and its recording land once the case-file UI and the real LLM call are in.
 118→
